85.title: The butter thief
85.hook: a toddler with butter on his chin, a line of happy monkeys, and the neighbors at his mother's door
85.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, often called Laddu Gopal, and bathe, dress and offer food to him each day; the butter-thief stories are told and sung, especially around Janmashtami.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a thread on a wrist, and a promise back. Today, the man who held Arjuna's reins, back when he was small enough to steal butter.

A village of cowherds on the banks of the Yamuna, early morning. The women have been churning since before dawn, and the fresh butter is hung high in clay pots, out of reach. It doesn't help. By noon a pot is cracked, the butter is gone, and a line of monkeys is licking their fingers. The culprit is about three years old. He has butter on his chin, and he swears he was asleep. The women march to his mother's door to complain, and halfway through complaining, they start laughing.
screen: `BUTTER, HUNG OUT OF REACH.` → `A LINE OF HAPPY MONKEYS.` → `HE SWEARS HE WAS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, the same Krishna you left holding Arjuna's reins on day seventy-seven. The Bhagavata Purana gives the neighbors' complaint as a list. He lets the calves loose before milking time. He steals the curd and the butter. He feeds it to the monkeys, and if the monkeys won't eat, he breaks the pot. When the pots are hung out of reach, he stacks up stools and a mortar and climbs. And when he's caught, he looks so innocent that nobody can stay angry. That's why the nickname stuck. In Hindi he's Makhan Chor, the butter thief, and it's always said with love. This same Krishna is honored as God. In the Gita he speaks as the source of everything, and in the same life he's a toddler being scolded by his mother. Devotees don't treat that as a contradiction. Many say it's the point: God close enough to be fed, chased, scolded and loved like a child. So Krishna comes with many faces. The baby born in a prison at midnight. The butter thief. The cowherd boy whose flute pulls the whole village outside. The friend driving a chariot onto a battlefield. Many people love one face most. In many homes there's a small brass baby Krishna, crawling, a sweet in one hand, often called Laddu Gopal. Families bathe him, dress him and offer him food each day, the way you'd care for a little child. Gopala means a cowherd, the one who looks after the cows. And the butter? Some devotees say it stands for a soft, well-churned heart, and that a heart is what he really comes to steal.
screen: `A THIEF THE WHOLE VILLAGE LOVES.` · `THE SAME KRISHNA, HONORED AS GOD.` · `ONE PERSON, MANY FACES.` · `THE BABY ON THE HOME SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Picture someone small you love caught mid-mischief, a child, a sibling, a pet: wide eyes, guilty grin, evidence on the chin. Notice the annoyance, maybe, and right under it something softer, and stay with the softer thing. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's child face in your mind the same way.
Makhan Chor. The butter thief: Krishna as a little boy, scolded and adored, and still honored as God. Today's word.
Your line: close enough to scold. A God you can chase around the kitchen. Day eighty-five, and the butter's gone.

86.title: The lopsided Ganesha
86.hook: a clay Ganesha made by hand, a little lopsided, and the worry that it isn't good enough
86.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
86.howItsDone: Many families bring home or make a clay Ganesha for Ganesh Chaturthi, often of natural clay so it dissolves at the immersion; in many pujas Ganesha is first invoked in a small cone of turmeric paste or a betel nut.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the butter thief, honored as God. Close enough to scold. Today, another small god, and a kitchen table covered in clay.

It's the week before Ganesh Chaturthi. Someone sits at the kitchen table with a lump of natural clay, because clay goes back to the earth when the festival ends. Two hours later there's a Ganesha. His trunk leans to one side. One ear is bigger than the other. The belly is great, though. Then they scroll past photos of other people's Ganeshas, smooth, painted, perfect, and the feeling turns. Embarrassed. A little jealous. Then guilty for being jealous. Someone online asked exactly this: am I a bad devotee? The answers came back warm. Today, the one people kept repeating.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, MADE BY HAND.` → `THE TRUNK LEANS.` → `AM I A BAD DEVOTEE?`

segments.voice: Start with the word for the figure itself: murti. It means a form, a body, a shape given to something. A murti isn't just a picture of God. Many Hindus understand it as a form God can be present in, and in many homes a short rite invites that presence before the worship begins. Temple murtis are often carved by trained craftsmen, following old rules for proportion. But look at what's honored at home. In many pujas, Ganesha is first called into a small cone of turmeric paste, or a single betel nut. No trunk. No ears. Shiva is widely worshiped as the lingam, a smooth rounded stone, and Vishnu as the shaligram, a dark stone from a riverbed in Nepal. Some of the most honored forms have no face at all. So what's being weighed? You met the verse on day eight. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. Nothing on that list is fine art. The love is the offering; the clay only carries it. And the jealousy? The people who answered said, gently, that feeling it is part of being a whole person, and noticing it is already something. Or, as people like to put it: Ganesha isn't an art critic. Like a parent with a child's drawing on the fridge, he sees who made it, and how. And a clay Ganesha that melts back into the water at the end of the festival? That isn't a flaw. That's the plan.
screen: `MURTI — A FORM, A BODY.` · `SOME HAVE NO FACE AT ALL.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `NOT AN ART CRITIC.`

segments.voice: Picture something you made, a drawing, a meal, a message, a messy first try, flaws and all. Notice the voice that starts comparing it to someone else's; let it talk without arguing, then remember who made it, and why. If you pray, you can offer it, crooked edges and all; if you don't, just let it be enough for now.
Murti. A form, a body: the shape in which God is honored, from carved stone to a cone of turmeric. Today's word.

87.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
87.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
87.howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, prayers and songs; in Gujarat people dance garba and dandiya, in Bengal Durga Puja is celebrated, and in the south homes display rows of dolls. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a lopsided clay Ganesha, and the murti, a form the love goes into. He's not an art critic. Today, the Goddess, and the rest of her story.

The buffalo demon is dead. You may know that story already: the gods' light pouring together into the Goddess, the lion, the shape-changing fight, her spear and sword at the end. On the nights of Navaratri, while Gujarat dances and Bengal builds its pavilions, the text that tells it, the Devi Mahatmya, is read aloud in homes and temples. And the text doesn't stop at the buffalo. A few chapters later, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven. Their servants bring word of a beautiful woman alone in the Himalayas. And the brothers make a very bad decision. They send her a marriage proposal.
screen: `THE TEXT DOESN'T STOP AT THE BUFFALO.` → `TWO DEMON BROTHERS.` → `A MARRIAGE PROPOSAL.`

segments.voice: Shumbha's messenger arrives with the offer. The king of the three worlds wants you, he says; all the treasures of heaven are his, and they could be yours. The Goddess answers politely. What you say is true, she tells him. But long ago I made a vow, a foolish one: whoever defeats me in battle, whoever breaks my pride, whoever is my equal in strength, he will be my husband. So tell your king to come and win me. The messenger can't believe it. A woman alone, against the lords of heaven? He goes back, and the brothers send an army. When the generals Chanda and Munda come for her, her face darkens with anger, and from her forehead springs Kali, gaunt and terrible, who destroys them both. So the Goddess gives Kali a name: Chamunda, the one who ended Chanda and Munda. One by one the army falls. Nishumbha falls. At the end Shumbha, the last, shouts at her: you're proud, but you only win because others fight for you. She answers: I am alone in the world here. Who else is there besides me? All the goddesses who fought beside her flow back into her body, and she faces him as one. Then she wins. Nava, nine; ratri, night. The text is read through these nights, and some households time it to finish by the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the victory. Notice the shape of the story. She keeps her word. She tells the truth about the terms. And when she's accused of borrowing her strength, she shows that every form was hers. Nine nights, then the dawn.

Answer it the way she answered the messenger, politely and on your own terms: not tonight. You don't need to win forever, just tonight, one night of nine.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day of victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. The Goddess wins on her own terms. Until tomorrow.

88.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
88.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
88.howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindus clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps on the new-moon night of Kartika, worship Lakshmi, open new account books, share sweets and visit family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, the Goddess, the buffalo demon, and nine long nights. Nine nights, then the dawn. Today, the darkest night of the month, and a row of little lamps.

You've heard Diwali's great story: Rama coming home to Ayodhya after fourteen years in the forest, and a city lighting lamps to show him the way. Tonight, look at the lamps themselves. It's the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, in autumn. No moon at all. On every windowsill, every doorstep, every railing, there's a small clay dish of oil with a cotton wick. Dozens of them. Hundreds, on a single street. Somebody's grandmother has been on her knees since the afternoon, drawing a pattern in colored powder at the front door. The door is wide open. Somebody is expected.
screen: `THE NEW-MOON NIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY SILL.` → `THE DOOR IS WIDE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Diwali is the everyday form of the Sanskrit Deepavali. Deepa is a lamp. Avali is a row. A row of lamps: the whole festival in two words. Not one big light, but a row of small ones, each a clay dish you could hold in your palm. And they come on the darkest night on purpose, the new moon of Kartika. If you wanted to show light winning, you'd pick exactly this night. So who is expected? Rama, in the Ramayana's story. And in many homes, on the main night, Lakshmi too, the Goddess of wealth and good fortune, of plenty in every sense. Families clean the house from top to bottom in the days before, because the tradition says she comes to homes that are clean, bright and open. They draw rangoli, those patterns of colored powder, at the threshold. Some paint small footprints walking in, as if she's already on her way. They leave doors and windows open and lamps burning so she can find the house. Shopkeepers close their old account books and open new ones with a prayer. The whole night is an act of welcome: a clean house, a lit path, an open door. And look at who the lamps are for. You can see your own house without them. They're for someone coming from outside, in the dark, looking for the way. Light the way home.

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp and turn the others off; if you can't, picture a clay lamp on your windowsill, and watch the flame. Think of the people who come home to you, or the ones you come home to: a partner on a late shift, a kid walking back from school, a parent you visit on Sundays. Picture your small light at the door, already lit, when they arrive.
Diwali. From Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the darkest night of Kartika for someone coming home.

89.title: Why is Krishna blue?
89.hook: the texts call Krishna, Rama and Draupadi dark; so why is he blue on the calendar and fair on the screen?
89.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
89.howItsDone: Devotional songs call Krishna Shyam or Ghanashyam, dark as a rain cloud; temple images show him dark, often black stone, and paintings usually show him blue; in Braj, Holi is played in his and Radha's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali: a row of lamps on the darkest night, and an open door. Your line was light the way home. Today, a question kids ask about the boy on the calendar.

Look at the calendar on almost any Hindu kitchen wall. Krishna is blue. Not a little blue: sky blue, peacock blue, swimming-pool blue. Now look at many of the films and TV shows made about him. Often he's played by a fair-skinned actor with a gym body. Then open the old texts. They agree with neither picture. So which one is he? Today, the color of the gods.
screen: `BLUE ON THE CALENDAR.` → `FAIR ON THE SCREEN.` → `WHAT DO THE TEXTS SAY?`

segments.voice: Start with his name. In Sanskrit, krishna means dark, even black. Some teachers also hear in it the one who draws you in, from a root that means to pull, and plenty of devotees happily keep both. But the color is right there in the name. The devotional poems call him Ghanashyam: dark as a rain cloud, the heavy blue-black cloud just before the monsoon breaks. In songs he's simply Shyam, the dark one. And he isn't alone. In the Ramayana, Rama too is described as dark. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi is called Krishnaa, the dark one, for her complexion, and Arjuna says one of his own names, Krishna, came from his dark skin. Dark, and in every case, beautiful. So where did the blue come from? Painters reached for the deep blue of a rain cloud, and over the centuries it brightened. Many devotees add a meaning: blue is the color of the sky and the ocean, the things with no edge. And the fair actors? Posters and films have often cast that way. The texts never asked for it. Many Hindus talk about this openly now, and nobody needs to blame one artist to see the gap. Braj even has a Holi story about it. Little Krishna is upset that he's dark and Radha is fair, and his mother tells him: go and color her face, and then you'll match. Notice what the story never says. It never says he should be lighter. It says: make everyone the same color for a day.
screen: `KRISHNA MEANS DARK.` · `DARK AS A RAIN CLOUD.` · `RAMA, DRAUPADI, ARJUNA TOO.` · `THE TEXTS NEVER ASKED FOR FAIR.`

segments.voice: Bring up the image of Krishna you grew up with, on a wall, a calendar, a screen, and notice its color. Then let it fade, and picture a monsoon sky: the heavy dark cloud just before the rain, the air cooling, everyone looking up, glad; that's the color the poets chose for the one they loved most. If your own skin is dark, or the skin of someone you love, let that be the color of the beloved for a few breaths.
Shyama. Dark, the dark one: a name for Krishna, dark as a rain cloud, and praised for it. Today's word.
Your line: dark as a rain cloud. In the old poems, that's a compliment. Day eighty-nine, done.

90.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
90.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
90.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
90.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a night-long vigil in Shiva temples, pour water, milk and bilva leaves over the lingam, and chant Om Namah Shivaya; many temple carvings show Shiva appearing from the pillar of light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shyama: Krishna, dark as a rain cloud, and praised for it. Today, Shiva's night again, and a pillar with no end.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says: I made everything, so I'm the greatest. Vishnu, the preserver, says: I hold everything together, so I am. It's an argument you could hear at any dinner table: who matters most. And it's getting heated. Then, between them, out of nowhere, a column of fire bursts up out of the ground. It rises past the clouds and goes down past anything they can see. No top, no bottom. Both of them stop talking.
screen: `WHO IS THE GREATEST?` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: This story is told in the Shiva Purana, and in others too. The two gods make a deal: whoever finds the end of the pillar wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for what the story calls ages. Vishnu never reaches the bottom. He comes back and says, honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma never reaches the top. On the way he sees a flower drifting down, and in many tellings he takes it back as proof and claims he found the top. He didn't. Then the pillar opens, and Shiva steps out of it. The light was him all along. In the tellings, Vishnu is honored for his honesty, and Brahma is rebuked for the lie. This is one of the stories people tell about the lingam, the rounded stone at the heart of a Shiva temple. Some understand it as a small image of that pillar of light: no beginning, no end. Some say this is the night it happened, the great night of Shiva. Others remember his wedding to Parvati, or his cosmic dance, on this night. Households hold these reasons side by side. Look at what the story is doing. The argument was about who was biggest. The answer was something neither of them could measure. The only right response was to stop, and pay attention. Stay awake for what matters.
screen: `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `NEITHER FINDS THE END.` · `THE PILLAR OPENS: SHIVA.` · `THE LINGAM, A PILLAR OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Picture the pillar of light, rising above you and going down below you, farther than you can follow; you don't have to reach the end of it, just stay with it. When the voice comes that says that's enough, take three more breaths. No boar, no swan, just staying.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva. For many, the night the pillar of light appeared, with no top and no bottom.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. The pillar has no end, and that's the point. See you tomorrow.

91.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

91.howItsDone: On Raksha Bandhan sisters tie rakhis on brothers, and in many regions family priests tie protective threads on the people they serve; the thread is also tied between friends, cousins and neighbors as a sign of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shivaratri: a pillar of light with no top and no bottom. Today, the thread again, and where it came from.

Some of the stories about the protective thread aren't about a brother and a sister at all. There's a king of the gods, going out to a war he's losing, and his wife, who won't let him go empty-handed. And much later, there's a province about to be split in two, where people walk into the street and tie threads on strangers. The rakhi glittering on cardboard in shop windows each summer has a longer, stranger history than the sibling ritual alone.
screen: `NOT ALWAYS A BROTHER AND SISTER.` → `A KING OF THE GODS AT WAR.` → `A PROVINCE ABOUT TO SPLIT.`

segments.voice: First, the king. A story told in the Bhavishya Purana, and repeated at many rakhi ceremonies, says that Indra, king of the gods, was being beaten by the demons. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, prepared a protective thread, blessed with sacred words, and tied it on his wrist on the full moon of Shravana. He went back into battle and won. So here the thread is tied by a wife on a husband, before a fight. Second, the priests. In many parts of India, on this same full moon, a family priest ties a protective thread on the wrists of the people he serves. The thread was never only one relationship. It's a blessing you can put on anyone you want to keep safe. Third, closer to our time. In 1905, the British government divided the province of Bengal. On the day the division took effect, the poet Rabindranath Tagore called on people to tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike, as a sign that the people of Bengal would not be split. People walked through Calcutta tying threads on neighbors and strangers. A wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister: what stays the same is the promise inside. And that's the week. A butter thief, a lopsided clay Ganesha, the Goddess's nine nights, the open door of Diwali, a boy dark as a rain cloud, a pillar of light, and a thread.
screen: `INDRANI TIES IT ON INDRA.` · `A PRIEST TIES IT ON HIS PEOPLE.` · `1905: THREADS ON STRANGERS.` · `THE PROMISE STAYS THE SAME.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Let a first face come, someone you'd protect, maybe the one from last time; then a second, someone who isn't family: a coworker going through something, a neighbor who lives alone, someone you disagree with. Picture tying a thread on their wrist too, and say inside: I'd look out for you. Stay with both faces for a few breaths.
Rakhi. The thread of protection, tied by a wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. Always holding a promise.
Your line: a thread can hold a promise. It was never only for brothers. That's day ninety-one.
